author: William Saville
reader_character: Jasper — adult first-person protagonist, externally they/them
title: Six Different Roads
subtitle: The Lanternweald — fifth expansion pass
content:
By the time I returned to Tideglass, I had tea leaves in one pocket, a spare bolt in another, and three appointments written on the back of a bakery receipt.

Maui examined the collection when I emptied it onto the kitchen table.

"Did you rob the village?"

"Only the parts that were freely offered."

He held up the bolt.

"Romantic."

"Danse thought it might help Tamsin with the shore gate."

"The tea?"

"Iroh gave me the last of the house blend for Fen."

"And the receipt?"

"That's my calendar, apparently."

He sat down.

"You're going to need a larger pocket."

I laughed, then stopped. I was exhausted in a way sleep alone wouldn't fix. I'd spent the last few days moving between districts, helping with the storm repairs and trying to keep promises to people I loved.

I wanted to tell Maui everything.

I didn't know where to begin.

He slid a cup toward me.

"Sit."

I sat.

"Tell me the part I should know," he said.

Not the part he had a right to own. Not every conversation, kiss, disagreement, or private fear from the other relationships.

The part I wanted to share.

I wrapped my hands around the cup.

"Severus and Neri are still reviewing the Closed Bells records. They found a scraped signature, but they won't guess whose it was."

"Good."

"Iroh's terrace drains were making strange sounds before the storm. He thinks the blocked service route may be pushing water into places it never used to go."

"Less good."

"Danse and Toph disagree about the shore gate, but they're finally using the same measurements."

Maui smiled.

"That sounds like a miracle."

"Don't call it that. They'll both be offended."

He laughed.

I told him Katara had returned from the South and was helping the clinic organize temporary supplies across the closed bridge. Aang was making sure the emergency travel rules didn't become an excuse to control people. Greg had offered to bring chairs and lanterns to the hall, but only after checking with the volunteers.

"And you?" Maui asked.

"What about me?"

"What did you need?"

I looked at the table.

That was the question I'd been avoiding.

I had spent so much energy helping other people have boundaries that I had begun treating my own as a nuisance.

"I need a day," I admitted. "A day where nobody asks me to hold a key, fix a schedule, or make a decision."

Maui nodded.

"Then let's have one."

"I don't want to cancel plans."

"Do you need to?"

I unfolded the bakery receipt. Two commitments could be moved without anyone suffering; the third was a clinic delivery that somebody else had already offered to cover.

I wrote three short notes.

Then I looked up.

"Are you sure you want to spend a day with me doing nothing useful?"

Maui grinned.

"I am a demigod. I can survive boredom."

"That remains untested."

We sent the notes before I could change my mind.

The next morning we slept late.

There were no bells. No urgent knocks. The sea was quiet enough that I could hear the wind moving through the little gaps around the window frame. Maui made breakfast with too much cinnamon and blamed the spoon.

I ate it anyway.

We walked along the upper ridge, where the storm had left seaweed tangled around the stones. The lower gate remained closed for inspection. The new garden beds were damp but intact, and Fen's little patch of wild flowers had survived.

Maui stopped beside the bench.

"Can I ask something difficult?" he said.

I nodded.

"Do you ever wish there were only one road?"

I looked out over the cove.

"Sometimes I wish the roads weren't so complicated."

"That's not what I asked."

"No."

He waited.

I spread the receipt on the table. The back was covered in small, unromantic obligations: a confirmed visit with Iroh, a message to Severus about the archive, a possible afternoon at Brasswatch, and a reminder to ask Katara whether the clinic still needed the clean blankets.

Maui stared. "It looks like an invasion plan."

"It's a calendar."

"Those are nearly the same."

I laughed and smoothed the curling paper. He leaned close without trying to read the parts I kept folded.

"Which of these actually affects us?" he asked.

"The visit I promised you on Saturday. The dinner I said I'd cook tonight. And the fact that I won't be here tomorrow morning."

He nodded, trying to take in the difference between knowing the important plans and knowing everything. We'd talked openly about my ethical non-monogamy and preference for polyamory; the trick was living that agreement when feelings weren't tidy.

"Can I say I want more of your Saturdays?" he asked.

"Yes. And I can tell you which ones I want to spend here."

"What if I don't like the answer?"

"Then we can be disappointed without punishing each other."

He considered that for a while. "Do you ever feel guilty because there are six roads?"

"Sometimes. Usually when I imagine somebody wants me to solve their sadness by giving away mine."

Maui's expression softened. "That sounds exhausting."

"It is."

He fetched the bowl of sea-glass stones we'd collected along the shore. He picked one, worn smooth and shaped a little like a heart, and set it beside the receipt.

"I don't want to be a road you have to walk because you promised."

"Then don't make yourself one."

"Could I be a place you choose to rest?"

The question caught me off guard. I reached for his hand.

"You already are," I said.

He smiled, quieter than usual. For a moment the kitchen was only a kitchen, full of crumbs and papers and two people learning not to count affection like a debt. Then he asked whose turn it was to wash the dishes, and the moment improved considerably.

I thought about the people I loved. Iroh's patient warmth. Severus's precise questions. Katara's steadiness, Aang's hope, and Toph's refusal to let anyone flatter her into silence. Danse learning to be a protector without a rank. Greg finding music in the quiet. Maui standing beside me, trying not to turn his own fear into a demand.

None of them was interchangeable.

"Do you wish I loved only you?" I asked.

He looked down.

"Sometimes I wish loving you were easier."

"Me too."

"But that's different from wanting you to be somebody else."

I took his hand.

"Yes."

He stared at our fingers.

"I don't need to know everything you do with everyone else," he said. "I want to know what affects us. When plans change. When you're afraid. When you want me close or need me to step back."

"That sounds fair."

"And I want you to tell me when I'm asking for too much."

"I will."

He smiled faintly.

"Even if I complain?"

"Especially then."

We sat on the bench for a long time.

The sea looked deceptively smooth from the ridge. Out beyond the harbor, the current still moved toward the old overflow channel. The second bell had not sounded since the storm.

I wasn't going to pretend that meant it was safe.

Maui leaned against me.

"Tell me something that has nothing to do with the village," he said.

I thought about it.

"Greg wrote a song that starts with the sound of a ferry bell."

"That's still the village."

"Severus puts his books in order by a system that makes sense only to him."

"That's probably a crime."

"Toph called my kite a potato."

He laughed so suddenly I nearly spilled my tea.

"Was it?"

"A graceful potato."

"Now I need to see it."

I pulled the little sketch from my notebook. He studied it with great seriousness.

"Terrible," he said.

"Thank you."

"Absolutely terrible."

I kissed him.

He caught my hand and kissed me again, slow and warm. The breeze lifted my hair, and the sun moved across the cove. For once I didn't feel the need to explain how this moment fit into the rest of my life.

It was part of it.

On the way home we stopped at the market. Mara had fresh bread. Fen was arguing with a supplier about the cost of rope. Lio showed us the corrected seat on the skiff and asked Maui to check a knot.

He did, then handed the line back.

No grand rescue.

At home, I took the bakery receipt from my pocket and copied the appointments into the proper calendar. I left a blank day for myself next week, without filling it immediately.

Maui noticed.

"Another day of doing nothing?"

"Maybe."

He smiled.

"Good."

That night I wrote a note in the green notebook I'd found in my old room.

I am not divided into six people because I love more than one.

I am one person with different roads to walk, and I get to decide when to rest.

Maui read the note only after I invited him.

He didn't add a speech.

He drew a tiny fish underneath, carrying a very large cup of tea.

I laughed and closed the book.
